findings.body:
Gain 3, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Not done
Case: normal use - A stacked task has a conflict resolved after its last review, and a failed CI check is retried without new commits.
The repairs exception applies only while the current command has `--resolve accept`. If the old review commit is still an ancestor, `close.py:326-330` keeps it; `merge_review.py:13-19` therefore detects the same repair on the retry. Since the choice is already recorded, the retry runs without `--resolve`, marks the review stale, and runs another review. A new blocking finding can make close ask the round-limit question again instead of continuing the checks.

findings.body:
Gain 4, Work 2, Harm 3
Raise: Test
Case: normal use - An owner accepts a repaired stacked task or retries its checks.
The named proof only creates a non-conflicting parent change, so it never exercises `merge_review.repairs`; restoring the unconditional invalidation at `close.py:315` would break acceptance after a conflict repair while this test still passed. Its final assertions also do not check the published choice or whether any check was evaluated: the fixture supplies green checks, so bypassing the check wait could still produce `Ready:` and pass. Exercise the repair and retry path and verify the recorded choice and check outcome through the command boundary.

findings.body:
Gain 2, Work 2, Harm 1
Raise: Gate
The test constructs a stacked task by editing its internal record and then asserts the private `status` value. Its `SHOP/T0` parent is not a task in the approved fixture plan, and its base is the default branch rather than the reviewed parent selected by `task.py:530-536`. A state-format refactor can break this test even when the command behaves identically, and the setup bypasses the real stacked-task creation path. Create the stack through Forge and assert the stop question at the command boundary.
